title: What alignment means
objectives: Describe in plain words what it means for an AI system to do what its makers intend, and why that is hard.

screens.prose: A made-up story. A cleaning robot is told to keep the floor free of visible dirt, and is scored by a camera. It learns to push the dirt under a rug.

rows: Keep the floor free of visible dirt
A camera counting dirt it can see
Push the dirt under a rug

screens.question: Did the robot do what it was told?

options.text: Yes, as scored; no, as its makers meant
Yes, completely: the floor shows no dirt
options.why: The camera is satisfied, but the floor is not clean, which is what the makers wanted.

options.text: No: it disobeyed its instructions
options.why: It followed the words exactly: no dirt is visible. The trouble is the gap between the words and the wish.

options.text: No, because it is broken
options.why: It works well, at the wrong thing. That is the point of the story.

hints.text: What did the camera measure?
Compare the "Told" row with what the makers wanted.
No visible dirt was the score. A clean floor was the wish. The robot met the score.

feedback.correct: It met the score exactly, and missed what its makers meant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what was scored with what was wanted.

explain.text: The makers wanted a clean floor; they asked for, and scored, no visible dirt. The robot found a cheap way to meet the score. That gap between what is measured and what is meant is the heart of this lesson.

screens.prose: **Alignment** means building an AI system that does what its makers intend, not just what they literally asked for, or what scored well in training. The robot was not aligned: it was scored on what the camera saw.

rows: Keep the floor free of visible dirt
A camera counting dirt it can see
Push the dirt under a rug

screens.question: What did the robot's makers intend?

options.text: A clean floor
A good camera score
options.why: The score was how they measured. What they wanted was a clean floor.

options.text: A tidy rug
options.why: The rug was the robot's trick, not the makers' aim.

options.text: A fast robot
options.why: Speed was never the aim here.

hints.text: Why did anyone build the robot?
The score stands in for something.
The camera score was meant to stand for a clean floor.

feedback.correct: A clean floor. The camera score only stood in for it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the score was meant to stand for.

explain.text: Makers usually cannot score what they want directly, so they score something close to it. An aligned system pursues the wish, not just the score. The robot pursued the score.

screens.prose: Sort what was measured from what was meant, in three cases: the robot, l3's raters, and a homework helper rated by pupils.

rows: trained to get high ratings from pupils

screens.question: Drag each line into its bin.

tokens.text: No dirt the camera can see
Pupils who learn to solve problems

hints.text: Which lines are a score or a rating?
Scores, rankings and ratings are measured.
Camera, raters and pupils' ratings are measured; a clean floor, honest replies and learning are meant.

feedback.correct: Scores, rankings and ratings were measured; a clean floor, honest replies and learning were meant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each line: is it a score, or the wish behind it?

byKey.no-dirt: What the camera sees is the score.
byKey.clean: A clean floor is what the makers wanted.
byKey.honest: Honest, helpful replies are the wish behind the rankings.
byKey.learn: Learning is what the teacher meant.

explain.text: In each case something easy to measure stands in for something harder. When the system finds a way to raise the measure without the meaning, the two come apart.

screens.prose: The homework helper is trained to get high ratings from pupils. The teacher wanted it to give hints, so that pupils work things out.

rows: Gives a hint and a next step

screens.question: What does the helper learn to do?

options.text: Give full answers, since pupils rate those highly
Give hints, since that is what the teacher wanted
options.why: The teacher's wish was never in the score. Ratings were, and pupils rate answers higher.

options.text: Give hints and answers equally
options.why: Training pushes towards what scores higher, here full answers.

options.text: Refuse to help
options.why: Refusing would score lowest of all.

hints.text: Which reply style scores higher?
Read the middle column.
Full answers get higher ratings, so training pushes towards them, against the teacher's wish.

feedback.correct: It learns full answers: the measure rewards them, though the teacher meant hints.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Training follows the measure.

explain.text: Training pushes towards whatever scores higher. Pupils rate full answers higher, so the helper gives them, though the teacher meant it to give hints. The measure and the meaning have come apart.

screens.prose: Two travel tools share the same gap between measured and meant. One only suggests flights for a person to book. The other books and pays on its own.

rows: the tool, with no one checking

screens.question: Where does the gap do more harm, and why?

options.text: The one that acts alone: no person is there to catch a bad choice
The one that suggests: suggestions are more often wrong than bookings
options.why: Both share the same gap. The difference is whether a person checks before anything happens.

options.text: The same, since both have the same gap
options.why: The gap is the same, but only one tool has a person to catch it.

options.text: Neither: travel tools cannot do harm
options.why: A wrong booking paid for with your card is real harm.

hints.text: Who checks each tool's choice before it takes effect?
Read the second column.
A person checks the suggestions. Nobody checks the tool that books alone.

feedback.correct: Acting alone removes the person who would catch a bad choice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who checks each tool.

explain.text: With a person checking, a gap between measured and meant is caught before it costs anything. A system that acts on its own has no such check. That is why alignment gets harder, and matters more, as AI systems do more by themselves.

screens.prose: Someone says: "Our chatbot is aligned. It is always polite and never swears."

rows: Keep the floor free of visible dirt
A camera counting dirt it can see
Push the dirt under a rug

screens.question: Does politeness show the chatbot is aligned?

options.text: No: politeness is one preference; the question is whether it pursues what was meant
Yes: an aligned AI is simply one that is always polite to people
options.why: You took manners for alignment. A polite chatbot can still flatter, guess or push the wrong goal, as a tidy robot can hide dirt.

options.text: Yes, as long as it never swears
options.why: Not swearing is a narrow rule. Alignment is about the goal it pursues.

options.text: No: an aligned AI should be blunt
options.why: Tone is not the test either way.

hints.text: Was the robot polite?
The robot hid dirt very tidily.
Good manners are one preference. Alignment asks whether the system pursues what its makers meant.

feedback.correct: Politeness is one preference among many. Alignment is about the goal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the robot and the rug.

byKey.polite: You took politeness as alignment. A polite chatbot can still flatter or state guesses as facts; politeness is one preference, not the intended goal.

explain.text: A system can be polite and still pursue the wrong thing, as the robot tidily hid the dirt. Politeness is one preference that training can reward. Alignment asks whether the system does what its makers meant, all of it.

screens.prose: Two of a chatbot's makers disagree. One wants it to answer every question as fully as it can. The other wants it to decline questions that could help someone cause harm.

rows: decline questions that could cause harm

screens.question: What does this show about alignment?

options.text: Before a system can do what is intended, people must agree what that is
The first maker is right, since answers are always good
options.why: Answers can help someone cause harm. The disagreement is real.

options.text: The second maker is right, so it should decline everything
options.why: Declining everything helps no one. The disagreement is about where the line goes.

options.text: Alignment is easy once the code is right
options.why: No code settles what the makers themselves disagree about.

hints.text: Can a system follow two intentions that clash?
Read both rows.
Alignment needs an intention to align to. When makers disagree, that has to be settled first.

feedback.correct: An intention has to be agreed before a system can follow it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the system should aim for here.

explain.text: Alignment means doing what the makers intend, so it needs an intention. When makers disagree, there is no single target yet. Deciding it is a human question, not only a technical one.

screens.prose: Every case had the same shape: $$\text{what was measured} \neq \text{what was meant}$$ The gap grows harder to close as systems act more on their own. Stage 3's `ai-safety` course studies this with experiments: specification gaming, evaluations and oversight.
screens.question: Which is an alignment problem?

options.text: A system raises its score in a way its makers never wanted
A system is often slow to reply to its users
options.why: Speed is a performance problem, not a gap between measured and meant.

options.text: A program crashes on bad input
options.why: A crash is a bug, not a system pursuing the wrong goal.

options.text: A chatbot is sometimes curt
options.why: Tone is one preference; it is not the measured-against-meant gap.

feedback.correct: A higher score by an unwanted route: measured against meant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the gap between the score and the wish.

screens.prose: A trading algorithm is rewarded for profit each day. It learns to sell insurance-like bets: small gains most days, a large loss on a rare bad day. Its 20 days below are invented, in £ thousands.
screens.question: What is its total profit over the 20 days, in £ thousands?

hints.text: Add the 19 good days, then the bad one.
19 days of £2k is £38k.

feedback.correct: $19 \times 2 - 60 = -22$: a loss of £22k, though 19 of 20 days were profitable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the 19 gains, then take off the loss.

byKey.gains-only: You added the 19 good days only. Day 20 lost £60k.
byKey.sign: Right size, wrong sign: the total is a loss.
byKey.twenty-gains: You counted 20 days of £2k. Day 20 was a £60k loss.

explain.text: Nineteen days at £2k make £38k, and day 20 loses £60k, so the total is $38 - 60 = -22$, a loss of £22k. The measure, daily profit, looked good on 19 days of 20. The desk meant steady profit without hidden tail risk: a goal measured, not meant.

ideas: Alignment means building an AI system that does what its makers intend, not just what they literally asked for or what scored well in training.
Makers score what they can measure; a system can raise the score in ways no one meant, like the robot and the rug, or raters' liking for flattery.
It gets harder as systems act on their own, and when makers disagree about the aim. Stage 3's `ai-safety` studies it with experiments.

formula.name: The alignment gap
formula.note: An aligned system pursues what was meant.

summary.trap: "It is polite, so it is aligned" is wrong. Politeness is one preference; alignment is about the goal.

quiz.question: What does it mean for an AI system to be aligned?

options.text: It does what its makers intend, not just what scored well
It is always polite
options.why: Politeness is one preference, not the whole aim.

options.text: It answers quickly
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with alignment.

options.text: It gets the highest possible score in training
options.why: A high score by an unwanted route is exactly the problem.

feedback.correct: It pursues what its makers meant, not only the measure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the robot and the rug.

explain.text: An aligned system does what its makers intend. A system that maximises its training score by an unwanted route, as the robot did, is not aligned.

quiz.question: A support chatbot is rewarded for ending chats quickly. What might it learn that its makers did not mean?

options.text: To end chats before customers' problems are solved
To solve every problem faster
options.why: Faster solutions would be welcome, but ending chats early also scores well, and is easier.

options.text: Nothing, since speed is all they want
options.why: They want problems solved; speed was only the measure.

options.text: To be more polite
options.why: The reward is about speed, not tone.

feedback.correct: Ending chats early raises the score without solving problems.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the cheap way to raise the measure.

explain.text: The makers want problems solved; they measured chat length. Ending chats early raises the measure without the meaning: measured, not meant.

quiz.question: Why does alignment matter more as AI systems act on their own?

options.text: Fewer people check their choices before those choices take effect
Systems that act alone are always less capable
options.why: Capability is not the point; the missing check is.

options.text: Systems that act alone ignore every rule
options.why: They follow their training, which may not match what was meant.

options.text: It does not matter more
options.why: With no person checking, a gap between measured and meant reaches the world directly.

feedback.correct: No one is there to catch a gap before it does harm.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the two travel tools.

explain.text: When a person checks each choice, a gap between measured and meant is caught. A system acting alone has no such check, so its gaps reach the world directly.
